newsitem.title: HONDURAS: One dead, 17 hurt in Honduras courthouse explosion.
newsitem.headline: One dead, 17 hurt in Honduras courthouse explosion.

text.p: A hand grenade exploded in Honduras' main courthouse on Thursday, killing at least one person and injuring 17, the Honduran Red Cross said.
"There is one person dead," Red Cross worker Marco Lozano told Reuters. "We transported 10 people, the fire department took three and five were taken off in private vehicles."
He said the total included Jose Ramos, a security guard at the building, who died in the blast. Among the injured were two children, two journalists, several lawyers and court officials, he said.
Wilfredo Alvarado, director of the judicial police's investigative unit, told reporters one person, a taxi driver, had been arrested.
Witnesses reported the explosion occurred at 11:20 a.m. (1720 GMT) when a fragmentation grenade was thrown from a passing car, police said. No group has claimed responsibility.

Officials immediately suspected that the explosion, which police earlier reported was a bomb, could have been a revenge attack against prosecutors who are seeking corruption charges against former President Rafael Callejas and his Cabinet.

"The enemies of the fight against impunity are now carrying out hateful and terroristic attacks," the country's top prosecutor, Edmundo Orellana, told reporters. "This has to be tied to the special cases that the Public Ministry is prosecuting."
But Orellana also speculated it could have come from a car-theft ring "that we have been hitting very hard."
The courthouse is the site of the Callejas case as well as proceedings against former army officers accused in the disappearance of leftist activists in the 1980s.

On Oct. 4, a bomb went off in the offices of the Honduran Congress, shattering windows but causing no injuries. That same day, police deactivated a bomb placed in the ruling Liberal Party headquarters.
A previously unknown group calling itself Hambre (Hunger) claimed responsibility for those bombings in a letter sent to Congress.
Honduras, one of the poorest countries in the hemisphere, is suffering from an economic crisis that many analysts say is pushing the country toward a social explosion.
